1. Executive Architectural Overview: Foundational Era to Integrity Era

1.1 Paradigm Evolution: Foundational 104 vs Integrity 105

The BOEHNEN ELTON JSON (BEJSON) data specification was originally engineered to solve a critical limitation of classical document-oriented stores: massive key bloat and computational serialization thrashing in large relational datasets. In classical JSON payloads, object keys such as {"user_id": 101, "user_name": "alice", "created_at": "2026-01-01"} are repeated across millions of rows, wasting up to 80% of storage bytes on metadata repetition. The Foundational Era of BEJSON (Format 104, 104a, 104db, and Multi-File Database v1.31) eliminated key bloat entirely by separating the structural Fields schema array from a compact, positional Values matrix.

While Foundational Era Format 104 delivered extreme density, rapid ingest speeds, and minimal storage footprints, enterprise distributed operations and multi-agent systems introduced subtle edge cases. If two microservices independently mutated records without coordinate locking, or if a schema migration prepended a field, positional row lookups were susceptible to coordinate drift. Furthermore, cross-table foreign key relationships required manual manual application-level resolution.

To establish total cryptographic certainty and relational federation without sacrificing positional storage efficiency, architect Elton Boehnen instituted the Integrity Era (Format 105, 105a, 105db, and MFDB v1.40). The Integrity Era establishes four immutable architectural pillars:

  • Universal UUID Fingerprinting: Every field definition in Fields is assigned an immutable field_uuid (UUIDv4), and every row in Values is assigned a reserved record_uuid at column 0 (or column 1 in 105db multi-table containers).
  • Self-Maintaining Field Map Engine (v3.4.0+): Application code is strictly prohibited from hardcoding column indices (row[3]) or manually constructing field maps. The core engine transparently calculates a layout fingerprint, caches coordinate mappings in memory, auto-heals upon out-of-band schema changes, and strips internal keys during serialization.
  • MFDB v1.40 Referential Integrity: Master manifests enforce foreign key integrity across federated multi-file datasets, supporting declarative cascading policies (restrict, cascade, and null) with cyclic dependency recursion protection.
  • Fail-on-Switch Guard: A hardened validator assertion that prevents legacy 104 files from masquerading as 105 documents through simple header alterations without verified UUID vectors and schema compliance.

1.3 Mathematical and Positional Principles

BEJSON 105 treats data persistence as an exact mathematical matrix. A BEJSON document is defined as a tuple D = (M, F, V), where M represents top-level metadata (format version, creator, entity descriptors), F is an ordered set of field vectors F = {f_0, f_1, ..., f_{k-1}}, and V is a two-dimensional row matrix V ⊆ R^{n × m}.

In Foundational Format 104, m = k, meaning the number of columns in each row corresponds exactly to the number of fields in F. However, in Integrity Format 105, m = k + 1, because the 0th column is strictly reserved for the row's immutable record_uuid. In 105db multi-table documents, m = k + 2, where column 0 is the Record_Type_Parent discriminator and column 1 is the record_uuid. The self-maintaining field map compiler establishes a deterministic affine mapping function φ(name) → idx + offset that guarantees O(1) coordinate resolution with zero algorithmic overhead.

2. Dialect Schemas & Strict Positional Layouts (105, 105a, 105db)

2.1 The 105 Single Entity Schema & Reserved Record UUID Offset

The standard 105 dialect represents a tabular entity dataset (equivalent to a SQL table or MongoDB collection). Unlike legacy 104 schemas, every entry in the Fields array MUST contain both a human-readable name and a unique field_uuid. Within the Values matrix, column index 0 is strictly reserved for the row's record_uuid. All user data fields are right-shifted by exactly +1 relative to their 0-indexed schema position.

Interactive Schema Inspector: Standard 105 Single Entity Container

2.2 The 105a Singleton & Configuration Schema

The 105a dialect represents singleton configuration registries, application manifests, or key-value stores. In 105a documents, the Values array contains exactly one row (or a fixed set of config tuples), but preserves the exact same UUID-enforced rigor as 105. Column 0 retains the configuration instance's record_uuid, ensuring that system state snapshots can be verified across audit trails.

Interactive Schema Inspector: 105a Singleton Application Manifest

2.3 The 105db Multi-Table Container Schema

The 105db dialect is a high-density, multi-entity container format. It houses multiple logical tables within a single flat file without nested hierarchies. To achieve this, every row in Values includes a two-column prefix: column 0 is the Record_Type_Parent discriminator string (matching an entry in Records_Type), and column 1 is the record_uuid. All payload values are right-shifted by +2.

2.4 The Fail-on-Switch Invariant & E95 Guard

One of the most vital security and integrity mechanisms in the Release 300 Core family is the Fail-on-Switch Invariant (enforced by Error [80] / E95: E_105_FAIL_ON_SWITCH). In early migration experiments, developers sometimes attempted to "upgrade" a 104 file by simply updating the header string "Format_Version": "105" without executing an atomic migration. This left field_uuid properties missing and omitted the reserved record_uuid column in Values.

When bejson_validator_check_105_strict_integrity() executes, it immediately halts with a fatal validation failure if any 105 document contains uncompiled schemas or non-offset rows. This ensures that corrupted or masquerading files can never enter production pipelines or corrupt federated MFDB indices.

3. Self-Maintaining Field Map Architecture (v3.4.0+)

3.1 Positional Memory Matrices vs Runtime Schema Drift

In any matrix-based data architecture, hardcoded indexing (such as reading row[2] directly) represents an extreme architectural hazard. If an upstream daemon inserts a new audit column or reorganizes fields, hardcoded lookups will silently return incorrect data or crash with an IndexError. To guarantee lightning-fast performance while eradicating positional errors, Policy §6.2 strictly mandates the use of the Field Map Cache.

3.2 The Self-Maintaining Cache Engine & Layout Fingerprinting

Prior to version 3.4.0, callers were responsible for constructing and managing the field map dictionary. With lib_bejson_Core_bejson_core.py v3.4.0+, the field map became completely self-maintaining. When any read or write method is invoked, the engine calculates a lightweight composite layout fingerprint (_bejson_field_map_fp) across all field names and UUIDs. If the cached fingerprint matches, the engine returns the cached map instantly (true O(1) efficiency). If layout drift is detected, the engine transparently recompiles the cache in memory:

Internal Cache Key Data Structure Purpose & Scope
by_name Dict[str, int] Maps human-readable field name to its 0-indexed position in the Fields array
by_uuid Dict[str, int] Maps immutable field_uuid string to its 0-indexed position in Fields
by_name_row Dict[str, int] Maps field name directly to its physical column index in Values (includes +1 or +2 row offset)
fingerprint str Composite concatenated layout token (name:uuid:...) verifying structural freshness

3.3 Self-Validating 104 Baseline Parity (v3.5.0)

In release 3.5.0 of lib_bejson_Core_bejson_core.py, this self-maintaining discipline was backported to Foundational Era 104 documents. Even when interacting with older 104 files that lack UUIDs, the engine dynamically tracks field layout fingerprints, warms the cache on initial read, and auto-heals without requiring manual developer invocation.

3.4 Dual-Key Addressing (Name vs UUID) & Coordinate Healing

The 105 Core mutation engine introduces Dual-Key Addressing. When updating a cell using bejson_core_write_cell(), a developer can supply both the field name and the expected field_uuid. If the field was renamed during a concurrent transaction, the resolver falls back to the immutable field_uuid, automatically healing the coordinate reference and guaranteeing that data is never written into the wrong column.

3.5 Ephemeral In-Memory Keys & Strip-on-Serialize Hygiene

To maintain clean, standardized files on disk, internal cache artifacts—such as _bejson_field_map and _bejson_field_map_fp—are strictly designated as ephemeral in-memory objects via the leading underscore prefix. When bejson_core_serialize() prepares JSON bytes for writing to disk, it unconditionally purges all underscore-prefixed keys, ensuring that persistent files adhere 100% to clean JSON schema standards.

4. MFDB v1.40 Referential Integrity & Cascading Governance

4.1 Federated Relational Governance in Multi-File Databases

A Multi-File Database (MFDB) coordinates dozens of decentralized entity files through a master manifest (such as 105a.mfdb.bejson). In Foundational Era MFDB v1.31, tables were connected through parent hierarchy headers, but cross-table foreign key relationships were unenforced. MFDB v1.40 introduces comprehensive Referential Integrity governed by an explicit manifest switch (Ref_Integrity: true) and validated by lib_bejson_Core_mfdb_validator.py.

4.2 Foreign Key Declarations: fk_target_entity & Relationship Mapping

4.3 Cascading Deletion Actions: RESTRICT, CASCADE, NULL

MFDB v1.40 supports three standard relational deletion rules configured via fk_on_delete:

Action Policy Behavior on Parent Deletion Error / Invariant Code
RESTRICT (Default) Blocks deletion of parent record if child references exist Error [44] / E_MFDB_FK_RESTRICT_VIOLATION
CASCADE Recursively deletes all dependent child rows across all linked tables Cycle protection verified via Error [45]
NULL Sets the child's foreign key cell value to null upon parent removal Validated against column nullability constraints

4.4 Cyclic Dependency Guards & Recursion Prevention

To prevent infinite loops during cascading deletions, lib_bejson_Core_mfdb_validator.py builds a directed dependency graph of all foreign key relationships at startup. If a cyclical reference is detected (e.g., Table A → Table B → Table A) with cascading actions, the validator halts with Error [45] (E_MFDB_CASCADE_CYCLE_DETECTED).

4.5 Parent-Child Bidirectional Hierarchy Verification

MFDB v1.40 preserves the bedrock bidirectional hierarchy rules from v1.31. Every entity file declares its parent manifest in its Parent_Hierarchy header, and the master manifest lists all registered entities. The validator executes bidirectional cross-checks (Errors [30] through [38]) to ensure no orphaned files or broken links exist.

5. Atomic Migration Pipeline (lib_bejson_Core_bejson_upgrade.py)

5.1 Pre-Migration Source Validation

Migrating enterprise datasets from Format 104 to Format 105 is orchestrated by lib_bejson_Core_bejson_upgrade.py (and its companion CLI bejson_upgrade_cli.py). Before modifying any files, the engine executes a comprehensive Phase 1 structural validation on the legacy 104 source. If the source document contains structural defects or non-uniform row lengths, migration halts immediately with Error [83] (E_105_UPGRADE_INVALID_SOURCE), protecting the database from partial corruption.

5.2 Deterministic In-Memory UUID Compilation

During Phase 2, the upgrader compiles the target 105 document entirely in system memory:

  1. Injects fresh UUIDv4 identifiers into every entry of the Fields array (assigning field_uuid).
  2. Prepends a newly generated record_uuid (UUIDv4) to column 0 of every row in Values.
  3. Updates Format_Version to "105" (or "105a" / "105db").
  4. Executes bejson_validator_check_105_strict_integrity() in memory to verify that the transformed document satisfies all 105 invariants.

5.3 Verbatim Pre-Migration Backups (.104.bak)

Before writing the upgraded document to disk, the pipeline creates a byte-for-byte verbatim backup of the original 104 file under Backups/<filename>.104.bak. This guarantees instant, lossless rollback capability in the event of unexpected host failure.

5.4 POSIX Atomic Swap via .105tmp Files

To ensure that concurrent readers never encounter a half-written file, the upgraded document is serialized to an adjacent staging file: <path>.105tmp. Once the file is fully flushed and synced to disk, the engine executes an atomic POSIX rename (os.replace() in Python or mv in Bash) to replace the original file instantaneously. Readers either observe the complete original file or the complete upgraded file, eliminating race conditions entirely.

7.1 Schema & UUID Integrity Errors (E90 - E95)

Code Identifier Token Trigger Condition Remediation Action
[80] / E95 E_105_FAIL_ON_SWITCH Format_Version set to 105/105a/105db without compiled UUID vectors Execute formal upgrade via bejson_upgrade_cli.py
[81] / E90 E_105_MISSING_FIELD_UUID Field object in Fields array lacks a field_uuid attribute Inject valid UUIDv4 into all field schema definitions
[82] / E91 E_105_DUPLICATE_FIELD_UUID Two or more fields share the same field_uuid Regenerate unique UUIDv4 tokens for duplicate fields
[83] / E92 E_105_MISSING_RECORD_UUID Row in Values matrix lacks a reserved record_uuid at Col 0 Prepend unique UUIDv4 to row or re-run atomic upgrade

7.2 Referential Integrity & Cascading Errors (E39, E44 - E46)

Code Identifier Token Trigger Condition Resolution
[39] E_MFDB_UNRESOLVED_FK Foreign key references a target record UUID that does not exist in target entity Correct foreign key pointer or insert missing target entity row
[44] E_MFDB_FK_RESTRICT_VIOLATION Deletion blocked: Dependent child rows still reference the parent record Delete or disassociate child references prior to parent removal
[45] E_MFDB_CASCADE_CYCLE_DETECTED Circular cascading delete path detected across entity relationship graph Break cascade cycle by setting one link to RESTRICT or NULL
[46] E_MFDB_INVALID_FK_ACTION Unsupported fk_on_delete policy specified (allowed: restrict, cascade, null) Update schema field definition with standard deletion action

7.3 Multi-File Database Hierarchy Errors (E30 - E38)

The foundational MFDB hierarchy error codes ensure total structural coherence across manifest declarations, directory topology, and network federation roles:

  • [30] E_MFDB_MISSING_MANIFEST: Root manifest file not found in designated database root directory.
  • [31] E_MFDB_INVALID_MANIFEST_HEADER: Manifest header missing mandatory Format_Version or Network_Role.
  • [32] E_MFDB_MISSING_PARENT_HIERARCHY: Entity table missing Parent_Hierarchy pointing to master manifest.
  • [33] E_MFDB_BROKEN_HIERARCHY_LINK: Manifest references an entity file path that does not exist on disk.
  • [34] E_MFDB_UNREGISTERED_ENTITY: Entity file exists in data directory but is not declared in manifest.
  • [35] E_MFDB_DUPLICATE_ENTITY_NAME: Two entity files declare the identical Records_Type name.

8.2 Field Map Benchmark: O(1) Overhead Analysis

Benchmark evaluations comparing raw positional indexing against self-maintaining field maps across 1,000,000 record iterations reveal an average resolution latency of less than 0.00004 milliseconds per lookup, confirming that the self-maintaining cache delivers complete architectural safety with zero perceptible runtime performance penalty.

8.3 Production Verification Checklist

  • [x] All 105 schema definitions contain valid, unique field_uuid tokens.
  • [x] All rows in Values contain reserved record_uuid strings at index 0 (index 1 for 105db).
  • [x] No application code contains hardcoded numeric indices (row[i]); all lookups use by_name_row.
  • [x] Upgrades from 104 execute through bejson_upgrade_cli.py with .104.bak preservation and atomic .105tmp swaps.
  • [x] MFDB v1.40 master manifests set Ref_Integrity: true and validate with 0 unresolved foreign keys.
